title: Why Users Go There: World Knowledge-Augmented Generative Next POI Recommendation

paper.title: Why Users Go There: World Knowledge-Augmented Generative Next POI Recommendation
paper.abstract:
Abstract Generative point-of-interest (POI) recommendation models based on large language models (LLMs) have shown promising results by formulating next POI prediction as a sequence generation task. However, the knowledge encoded in these models remains fixed after training, making them unable to perceive evolving real-world conditions that shape user mobility decisions, such as local events and cultural trends. To bridge this gap, we propose AWARE (Agent-based World knowledge Augmented REcommendation), which employs an LLM agent to generate location- and time-aware contextual narratives that capture regional cultural
characteristics, seasonal trends, and ongoing events relevant to each user. Rather than introducing generic or noisy information, AWARE further anchors these narratives in each user’s behavioral context, grounding external world knowledge in personalized spatial-temporal patterns. Extensive experiments on three real-world datasets demonstrate that AWARE consistently outperforms competitive baselines, achieving up to 12.4% relative improvement.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: With the proliferation of location-based social networks (LBSNs) and mobile devices, massive volumes of user check-in data have become available, enabling the study of human mobility at an unprecedented scale Gonzalez et al. (2008) . A central task in this domain is next point-of-interest (POI) recommendation : given a user’s historical check-in trajectory, predicting the most likely next location they will visit Li et al. (2024) ; Feng et al. (2024a) ; Halder et al. (2022) ; Zhong et al. (2025) . Accurate next POI prediction directly benefits real-world applications, including personalized navigation, location-aware advertising, and urban planning Zheng (2015) , and has attracted increasing attention from both academia and industry in recent years. Figure 1: Comparison of (a) traditional generative recommendation using only historical check-in data, and (b) AWARE, which augments the GR model with dynamic world knowledge selected by an LLM agent. Existing approaches have evolved from collaborative filtering and Markov chain models Feng et al. (2015) to recurrent and attention-based architectures Hochreiter and Schmidhuber (1997) ; Luo et al. (2021) ; Yang et al. (2022) ; Yan et al. (2023) that capture increasingly complex spatial-temporal dependencies. More recently, large language models (LLMs) Ding et al. (2026) ; Rajput et al. (2023) ; Chen et al. (2025) ; Jiang et al. (2026) ; Zhou et al. (2025) have given rise to generative POI recommendation Li et al. (2024) ; Wang et al. (2025) ; Liu et al. (2025) ; Lv et al. (2026) , which serializes check-in history into a natural language prompt and fine-tunes an LLM to directly generate the next POI. By exploiting rich textual representations rather than opaque ID embeddings, generative approaches achieve strong performance on next POI prediction benchmarks. Despite their promise, existing generative POI recommendation models share a critical limitation: once fine-tuned on historical data, they operate as static systems whose knowledge is entirely frozen at training time. This renders them unable to capture evolving real-world context, such as local events, cultural trends, and seasonal shifts, that fundamentally shapes user mobility decisions. For example, a user who routinely visits a gym on weekday evenings may instead attend a community fitness event at a nearby park; a static model, unaware of this event, would confidently predict the gym and fail. Without access to such external context, existing methods capture where users have been but not why they go next. To address this gap, we propose AWARE ( A gent-based W orld- A ugmented RE commendation), a framework that injects dynamic, personalized world knowledge into the generative recommendation pipeline (Figure 1 ). For each user’s activity region and time period, AWARE employs an LLM agent to synthesize contextual narratives, termed hotspot text , describing regional cultural characteristics, seasonal trends, and ongoing events. Unlike RAG, which returns pre-indexed documents irrespective of user identity, our agent reasons over each user’s mobility history to produce personalized narratives that distill relevant world context into actionable conclusions. To ensure the injected knowledge remains user-specific rather than generic, AWARE further anchors the hotspot text in behavioral signals such as frequently visited locations and habitual spatial transitions.

sections.heading: 2.1 Problem Formulation
sections.text: Let 𝒰 \mathcal{U} denote the set of users and 𝒫 \mathcal{P} the set of POIs. Each POI p ∈ 𝒫 p\in\mathcal{P} is associated with a name, a category, and geographic coordinates. A check-in ( u , p , t ) (u,p,t) records that user u u visited POI p p at time t t . For each user u u , the check-in history is an ordered sequence 𝒮 u = [ ( p 1 , t 1 ) , ( p 2 , t 2 ) , … , ( p n , t n ) ] \mathcal{S}_{u}=[(p_{1},t_{1}),(p_{2},t_{2}),\ldots,(p_{n},t_{n})] . The task is to predict the next POI p n + 1 p_{n+1} given 𝒮 u \mathcal{S}_{u} and the current time context. Figure 2: Overview of the AWARE framework. (1) An LLM agent retrieves external signals (e.g., news, events, festivals) and integrates them with user behavioral patterns to produce personalized narratives. (2) The pretrained GR model is fine-tuned with the acquired world knowledge to generate context-aware recommendations.

sections.heading: 2.2 Generative POI Recommendation
sections.text: Recent work reframes next POI prediction as a text generation task Li et al. (2024) ; Wang et al. (2025) ; Liu et al. (2025) ; Lv et al. (2026) . A user’s check-in history is serialized into a structured prompt containing POI names, categories, timestamps, and geographic information. An LLM is then fine-tuned to generate the next POI as its output sequence. Formally, a prompt construction function ϕ ⁡ ( ⋅ ) \phi(\cdot) converts 𝒮 u \mathcal{S}_{u} into a textual input x = ϕ ⁡ ( 𝒮 u ) x=\phi(\mathcal{S}_{u}) , and the model is trained to maximize P ⁡ ( y ∣ x ) P(y\mid x) , where y y is the ground-truth next POI. This formulation enables the model to leverage pre-trained semantic knowledge about location names and categories, providing richer representations than ID-based.

sections.heading: 2.3 Semantic ID
sections.text: Rather than representing POIs by raw names, which consume lengthy token sequences and lack structural relationships, recent work assigns each POI a compact Semantic ID (SID) Wang et al. (2025) . SID encodes each POI as a short compositional token sequence whose components capture different facets and can be shared across POIs: Coffee Shop, 1128 3rd Ave ⇒ \Rightarrow <a_29><b_31><c_20> Coffee Shop, 5 W 21st St ⇒ \Rightarrow <a_26><b_3><c_20> Both POIs share <c_20> due to their common category, while the remaining tokens capture individual identity. AWARE is agnostic to the POI representation scheme; in this work we adopt a SID-equipped generative backbone (details in Section 3 ).

sections.heading: 2.4 World Knowledge for POI Recommendation
sections.text: In this work, world knowledge refers to dynamic, location-specific contextual information beyond check-in records, including regional cultural characteristics, local events, and seasonal trends. Such knowledge evolves continuously and often drives user mobility decisions, yet cannot be encoded statically within model parameters. We define world knowledge as w = 𝒜 ⁡ ( 𝒮 u , l , t ) w=\mathcal{A}(\mathcal{S}_{u},l,t) , where 𝒜 \mathcal{A} denotes an LLM agent, l l is the user’s activity region, and t t is a temporal context. Unlike generic knowledge retrieval, 𝒜 \mathcal{A} first analyzes the user’s mobility patterns from 𝒮 u \mathcal{S}_{u} , then incorporates real-world events and trends relevant to region l l at time t t . For example, given a user who commutes between Queens and Midtown Manhattan and has visited Yankee Stadium on weekends during April–May 2012, the agent may generate: “The user exhibits a commuting pattern between Queens and Midtown Manhattan. Combined with the Yankees’ home season in April–May, the user is likely interested in upcoming home games or nearby venues.” We term this output hotspot text , a personalized narrative that bridges user behavior with external world dynamics to reason about why a user is likely to visit certain POIs.

sections.heading: 3 Methodology
sections.text: In this section, we present the AWARE framework (see Figure 2 ). We first describe the personalized world knowledge acquisition (Section 3.1 ), then introduce user-aware knowledge alignment (Section 3.2 ), and finally detail the context-aware generative inference (Section 3.3 ).

sections.heading: 3.1 World Knowledge Acquisition Agent
sections.text: Existing generative POI models treat knowledge as static, yet user mobility is shaped by evolving real-world dynamics that no fixed-parameter model can capture. External sources such as news feeds, event calendars, and travel portals offer a natural remedy, but their content is vast and largely irrelevant to any individual user. This motivates AWARE’s design principle: leveraging each user’s behavioral patterns as an anchor for world knowledge selection, so that the distilled signals capture not only where users have been but why they are likely to go next.

sections.heading: 3.1.1 Three-Stage Reasoning Strategy
sections.text: To this end, AWARE instantiates a tool-augmented LLM agent 𝒜 \mathcal{A} that, given a user’s trajectory 𝒮 u \mathcal{S}_{u} and the temporal–spatial context ( t , l ) (t,l) implied by the tail of the trajectory, is equipped with a retrieval toolbox ℛ = { web_search , web_fetch } \mathcal{R}=\{\texttt{web\_search},\,\texttt{web\_fetch}\} and produces a compact hotspot text: w = 𝒜 ⁡ ( 𝒮 u , t , l , ℛ , Π ) , w=\mathcal{A}\bigl(\mathcal{S}_{u},\,t,\,l\,;\,\mathcal{R},\,\Pi\bigr), (1) where Π \Pi denotes the system prompt that governs the agent’s reasoning protocol. The protocol decomposes into three sequential stages, with a detailed description provided below.

sections.heading: Stage (i): Behavioral Profile Inference.
sections.text: The agent first parses 𝒮 u \mathcal{S}_{u} in chronological order and weights the tail of the sequence more heavily to identify the user’s active neighborhood l l , recurring interests (e.g., dining style, commute routine, fitness habits, nightlife preferences), and plausible near-term intent. This profile is retained as an internal anchor and never exposed verbatim in the final output, ensuring that downstream retrieval is driven by user-specific priors rather than generic demographic assumptions.

sections.heading: Stage (ii): Constrained External Retrieval.
sections.text: Conditioned on the inferred profile, the agent formulates targeted web queries that jointly bind three constraints: geographic (restricted to l l and its surrounding neighborhoods), temporal (anchored at t t , with the target year and month embedded explicitly in every query), and thematic (the inferred interest categories). Retrieval proceeds iteratively: broader web_search calls first surface candidate event calendars, neighborhood guides, and news items, after which web_fetch verifies specific claims on the most informative pages. The agent is explicitly instructed to corroborate each substantive claim across at least two independent sources and to discard any signal that cannot be anchored to the target time window, which mitigates hallucinations inherited from the LLM’s parametric memory.

sections.heading: Stage (iii): Grounded Synthesis.
sections.text: In the final stage, the agent weaves the internal behavioral anchor together with the verified external signals into a single coherent paragraph w w . The paragraph is required to interleave three elements in a tightly integrated manner: (a) what the user’s history suggests, (b) what regional context is salient at time t t , and (c) what POI categories or venue styles the user is most likely to seek next. Outputs that merely recite the trajectory, or that read as generic city guides disconnected from user behavior, are rejected by the format constraints in Π \Pi , ensuring that w w reads as a user-grounded contextual interpretation rather than a document summary.

sections.heading: 3.1.2 Agent Instantiation and Prompt Design
sections.text: We instantiate 𝒜 \mathcal{A} with a large-capacity LLM ( Qwen3-max ) augmented with a web-retrieval toolbox ℛ \mathcal{R} that provides date-filtered web search and page-level content extraction. The system prompt Π \Pi encodes the three-stage protocol as explicit instructions and imposes three key constraints: (i) all factual claims must be grounded in retrieved evidence rather than parametric memory, (ii) the output must be a single coherent paragraph, and (iii) the length must not exceed a word budget M M , which can be adjusted according to application requirements. Figure 3 visualizes the key components of Π \Pi , including the quality safeguards elaborated in Section 3.1.3 . The complete system prompt is provided in Appendix C . Tools. web_search (with publication-date filter) and web_fetch . Protocol. (1) Infer user preferences, routines, and near-term intent from 𝒮 u \mathcal{S}_{u} (tail-weighted). (2) Identify the active region and activity context. (3) Issue parallel queries for region- and time-local hotspots, events, and trends. (4) Synthesize one paragraph weaving behavior, context, and predicted POI categories. Temporal fidelity. Treat the latest timestamp in 𝒮 u \mathcal{S}_{u} as “now”; embed the target year/month in every query; prefer archival sources; drop unverifiable claims. Search budget. At most two retrieval rounds; emit parallel queries rather than serial refinements. Output. One compact English paragraph ( ≤ M \leq M words); no structured formatting or trajectory recitation. sections.heading: 3.1.3 Generation Quality Control
sections.text: Beyond the reasoning protocol, AWARE enforces three operational constraints on agent outputs, namely output-format control , tool-usage efficiency , and temporal fidelity , each implemented across prompt, tool, and post-hoc validation layers to forestall any single failure mode.

sections.heading: Output-Format Control.
sections.text: Since the downstream GR model is prompt-length sensitive, we enforce the word budget M M via a prompt, validator, and truncator cascade: Π \Pi instructs the agent to cap w w at M M words and self-check length; if the validator detects | w | > M |w|>M , the agent is re-invoked with a brief rewrite instruction; any residual overshoot is hard-truncated. We instantiate two budgets, M = 80 M=80 and M = 150 M=150 , which anchor the informativeness versus noise trade-off in Section 4.5 .

sections.heading: Tool Usage Efficiency.
sections.text: Since agent rollouts dominate preprocessing cost, Π \Pi caps retrieval at two rounds, a broad main round and an optional supplemental round for residual gaps, and encourages parallel rather than sequential queries within each round; our orchestrator dispatches them concurrently. A code-level guard hard-stops any attempt at a third round and forces synthesis, bounding per-user latency and cost.

sections.heading: Temporal Fidelity.
sections.text: As the evaluation benchmarks span 2009 to 2013 and predate contemporary LLM training corpora, AWARE grounds the agent in the user’s own timeline: the latest timestamp in 𝒮 u \mathcal{S}_{u} is treated as “now,” every query is anchored to the target year and month, and documents lacking period-appropriate corroboration are discarded, ensuring that the injected knowledge reflects the user’s original temporal and spatial context.

sections.heading: 3.2 User-Aware Knowledge Alignment
sections.text: Indiscriminate injection of world knowledge risks introducing noise. To ensure that external context is actionable for each user, AWARE aligns world knowledge with user-specific behavioral evidence through three complementary priors. Frequency-Based Behavioral Prior. We compute a frequency-ranked list of each user’s visited POIs: ℱ u = [ ( p 1 , c 1 , f 1 ) , ( p 2 , c 2 , f 2 ) , … ] \mathcal{F}_{u}=[(p_{1},c_{1},f_{1}),(p_{2},c_{2},f_{2}),\ldots] (2) where p i p_{i} denotes a POI, c i c_{i} its category, and f i f_{i} the visit count. This prior encodes long-term behavioral regularities and serves as a relevance filter: signals aligning with established patterns receive implicit reinforcement, while those lacking behavioral corroboration are down-weighted. Transition-Based Spatial Grounding. We model user mobility dynamics by extracting POI-to-POI transition statistics. For each POI p i p_{i} visited by user u u , we record the set of subsequent destinations and their frequencies: 𝒯 u ​ ( p i ) = { ( p j , n i ​ j ) } j = 1 | 𝒩 ⁡ ( p i ) | \mathcal{T}_{u}(p_{i})=\{(p_{j},n_{ij})\}_{j=1}^{|\mathcal{N}(p_{i})|} (3) where p j p_{j} is a destination POI and n i ​ j n_{ij} the transition count. Given the most recently visited POI, we select the top- k k most frequent transitions as spatial grounding signals, channeling world knowledge through the user’s movement structure. Periodic Temporal Modeling. User mobility often exhibits strong periodicity : behavior on Monday mornings is more predictive of next Monday than activity from the preceding weekend. To capture such long-range periodic evidence, AWARE reserves a fraction β \beta of the history budget for entries sharing the same day-of-week as the prediction target, filling the remaining slots with the most recent entries. Formally, given budget L L and target day-of-week d d , we select ⌊ β ​ L ⌋ \lfloor\beta L\rfloor entries from { e ∈ 𝒮 u ∣ dow ​ ( e ) = d } \{e\in\mathcal{S}_{u}\mid\text{dow}(e)=d\} and ( L − ⌊ β ​ L ⌋ ) (L-\lfloor\beta L\rfloor) recent entries from the remainder. This ensures that temporal knowledge from the agent (e.g., “Friday evening trends”) is paired with the user’s corresponding historical behavior.

sections.heading: 3.3 Context-Aware Generative Inference
sections.text: Before describing how AWARE constructs its input, we briefly outline the generative recommendation (GR) pipeline. Each POI is assigned an SID by embedding its textual description through a pretrained language model and discretizing via hierarchical clustering. A geospatial prefix derived from S2 cells Google Inc. (2023) is prepended to encode geographic locality at multiple resolutions, enabling spatially proximate POIs to share prefix tokens. The model is trained to generate the ground-truth next POI’s SID given the user’s historical sequence, and autoregressively produces the predicted SID at inference time Lv et al. (2026) . Building on this pipeline, AWARE organizes the acquired knowledge (Sec. 3.2 ) into a structured prompt providing three complementary dimensions beyond the check-in sequence: x = ϕ ⁡ ( ℋ u , ℱ u , w , 𝒞 u , 𝒯 u ) x=\phi(\mathcal{H}_{u},\mathcal{F}_{u},w,\mathcal{C}_{u},\mathcal{T}_{u}) (4) where ℋ u \mathcal{H}_{u} denotes the time-aware historical trajectories, ℱ u \mathcal{F}_{u} the POI visit frequency statistics, w w the generated world knowledge, 𝒞 u \mathcal{C}_{u} the current trajectory to be continued, and 𝒯 u \mathcal{T}_{u} the transition pattern conditioned on the last visited POI. A complete prompt example is provided in Appendix B . To accommodate the knowledge-enriched input, we fine-tune the backbone with LoRA Hu et al. (2022) , optimizing the generation objective over ground-truth next POI y y given prompt x x : ℒ = − log ⁡ P θ ​ ( y ∣ x ) \mathcal{L}=-\log P_{\theta}(y\mid x) (5) Since AWARE operates entirely at the input representation level, it requires no architectural modification to the backbone and is orthogonal to downstream reasoning stages such as Chain-of-Thought and reinforcement learning, whose benefits can be combined additively.

sections.heading: 4.1 Experimental Setting
sections.text: Datasets. We evaluate AWARE on three real-world LBSN datasets that are widely adopted in next POI recommendation research: Foursquare-NYC , Foursquare-TKY Yang et al. (2015) , and Gowalla-CA Cho et al. (2011) . These datasets span diverse urban environments with varying scales of user activity and POI catalogs, providing a comprehensive testbed for evaluating recommendation methods across different mobility contexts. Detailed dataset preprocessing and statistics are summarized in Appendix A . Baselines. To comprehensively assess the effectiveness of AWARE, we compare against representative baselines spanning three categories: (i) Traditional method: PRME Feng et al. (2015) , which learns metric embeddings for next-step transition prediction; (ii) Neural-based methods: GETNext Yang et al. (2022) , TPG Luo et al. (2023) , MTNet Hu et al. (2018) , STHGCN Yan et al. (2023) , and ROTAN Feng et al. (2024b) , which employ graph networks, attention mechanisms, or specialized spatio-temporal encoders to model sequential mobility patterns; and (iii) LLM-based methods: SpaceTime-GR Lin et al. (2025) , LLM4POI Li et al. (2024) , GNPR-SID Wang et al. (2025) , GA-LLM Liu et al. (2025) , CoAST Zhai et al. (2025) , and ROS Lv et al. (2026) , which reformulate next POI prediction as a sequence generation task using large language models with varying strategies for spatial reasoning. Detailed descriptions of all baselines are provided in Appendix D . AWARE consistently outperforms ROS across all three datasets, achieving relative improvements of 6.0% on NYC, 6.5% on TKY, and 12.4% on CA. sections.heading: 4.3 Ablation Study
sections.text: Table 2 reports the ablation results on the NYC dataset, organized into two groups: the world knowledge acquisition agent and the user-level behavioral signals.

sections.heading: World Knowledge Acquisition Agent.
sections.text: The upper block of Table 2 investigates whether the gains stem from agent-based synthesis or merely from richer prompt context. Removing all world knowledge yields a − 3.1 % -3.1\% drop, confirming its indispensable role. Notably, replacing synthesized text with raw search snippets causes an even larger drop ( − 3.3 % -3.3\% ), indicating that unprocessed retrieval introduces harmful noise. Retaining only parametric summarization ( − 2.9 % -2.9\% ) and generating non-personalized city-level descriptions ( − 2.4 % -2.4\% ) further confirm that external retrieval, agent-mediated synthesis, and user-level personalization are all necessary, and that the improvement cannot be attributed to prompt expansion alone.

sections.heading: User-Level Behavioral Signals.
sections.text: All three behavioral signals produce comparable degradation when removed ( − 2.0 % -2.0\% to − 2.2 % -2.2\% ), suggesting that each captures a distinct aspect of user mobility. The behavioral priors collectively account for substantial gains ( − 2.3 % -2.3\% ), indicating that grounding world knowledge in user-specific spatial-temporal patterns is essential for effective knowledge injection, as illustrated in our case study (Appendix F ).

sections.heading: 4.5 Hotspot Text Length Analysis
sections.text: Since the granularity of world knowledge is controlled by the length of the hotspot text, we train separate models with the agent constrained to at most 80 and 150 words. As shown in Figure 4 , world knowledge exhibits a clear length–quality relationship: the 80-word configuration (0.4050) offers only marginal improvement over the variant without hotspot text (0.4029 in Table 2 ), while the 150-word variant (0.4160) yields substantial and consistent gains across all three cities, with the improvement widening on sparser data (CA: +7.4% from 80 to 150 words). This validates the agent-based design: producing sufficiently grounded narratives requires contextual reasoning over user behavior and external signals, a capability that arises naturally from the LLM agent’s generative process. sections.heading: 4.6 Cross-City Generalization
sections.text: To evaluate whether world knowledge facilitates transfer across cities, we train all models on NYC and directly evaluate on TKY and CA without any adaptation. As shown in Figure 5 , AWARE consistently outperforms all baselines on both in-city and cross-city. We attribute this to the nature of world knowledge: the LLM agent encodes contextual information as natural language narratives describing general human mobility patterns, cultural habits, and temporal regularities, which are inherently not city-specific. This language-level generality allows AWARE to transfer meaningful contextual signals across geographic boundaries, complementing the structural transferability of the shared semantic space.

sections.heading: 4.7 Top-K Recommendation Quality
sections.text: Beyond top-1 accuracy, Table 4 reports HR@ K K and NDCG@ K K for K ∈ { 5 , 10 , 20 } K\in\{5,10,20\} on NYC. AWARE surpasses not only ROS but also ROS full , which additionally incorporates Mobility CoT and spatial-guided RL. The margin widens at higher K K (e.g., HR@20: +15.8% over ROS), suggesting that world knowledge enriches the candidate space with contextually plausible POIs that reasoning-level enhancement alone cannot recover.

sections.heading: 4.8 Prediction Distance Distribution
sections.text: A natural concern is whether external knowledge introduces spatial noise. As shown in Figure 6 , both methods perform comparably at P50 and P75, confirming that world knowledge does not degrade spatial precision. The difference emerges in the tail (P90: 8.44 vs. 9.20 km; mean: − 3.4 % -3.4\% ), where AWARE produces fewer large-error predictions by resolving spatially ambiguous cases.

sections.heading: 5 Related Work
sections.text: Next POI Recommendation. Next POI recommendation has evolved from metric embeddings Feng et al. (2015) and recurrent architectures Hochreiter and Schmidhuber (1997) to attention-based Luo et al. (2021) , graph-enhanced Yang et al. (2022) , and hypergraph methods Yan et al. (2023) . More recently, LLM-based approaches reformulate the task as sequence generation, with representative work including LLM4POI Li et al. (2024) , GNPR-SID Wang et al. (2025) , CoAST Zhai et al. (2025) , GA-LLM Liu et al. (2025) , and ROS Lv et al. (2026) . Knowledge-Enhanced Recommendation. Prior POI recommendation work has leveraged geographic knowledge such as street-level addresses Lv et al. (2026) , category taxonomies Wang et al. (2025) , and spatial distance constraints Liu et al. (2025) . However, these sources are predominantly static and do not capture the dynamic real-world context that often drives user mobility decisions. LLM Agents for Information Acquisition. Agent-based approaches such as RecMind Wang et al. (2024) employ the LLM as the recommender itself, performing multi-step reasoning at inference time Yao et al. (2023) . While effective, this design couples reasoning cost with serving latency and forgoes the ability to learn fine-grained behavioral patterns from large-scale training data. Different from methods above, AWARE uses the LLM agent solely for offline knowledge acquisition, allowing the generative backbone to internalize dynamic world knowledge through supervised learning and adapt it to individual user contexts.

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: We present AWARE, a framework that acquires world knowledge via an LLM agent, personalizes it through behavioral priors, and injects it into generative POI recommendation to capture context-dependent mobility intent. Experiments across multiple datasets show consistent gains over competitive baselines, and ablations confirm that the two signals are complementary, revealing not only where users have been but why they will go next.

sections.heading: Limitations
sections.text: AWARE currently acquires world knowledge in an offline, pre-training stage: hotspot text is generated once per user and remains fixed throughout training and inference. While this design ensures zero additional latency at serving time, it cannot capture events that emerge after the knowledge acquisition pass. Extending the framework to support incremental or online knowledge refresh, where the agent periodically updates narratives in response to newly occurring events, would further improve temporal coverage. Additionally, the current agent relies on web search as its primary evidence source, which may offer uneven coverage across geographic regions and languages. Incorporating structured knowledge bases such as event calendars and transportation schedules could improve robustness in regions where web coverage is sparse.

sections.heading: Appendix D Baseline Descriptions
sections.text: We provide detailed descriptions of all baseline methods compared in our experiments.

sections.heading: PRME.
sections.text: PRME Feng et al. (2015) learns user and POI embeddings in a shared metric space, where next-step transitions are predicted by ranking candidate POIs based on their distance to the user’s current state. It captures sequential transition patterns through pairwise learning-to-rank objectives.

sections.heading: GETNext.
sections.text: GETNext Yang et al. (2022) employs a graph-enhanced transformer architecture for next POI recommendation. It constructs a global POI transition graph to capture collaborative transition patterns and integrates spatial and temporal information through dedicated embedding layers, combining graph-level structural signals with transformer-based sequential modeling.

sections.heading: TPG.
sections.text: TPG Luo et al. (2023) incorporates fine-grained temporal information into POI recommendation by encoding timestamps as continuous features. It models the temporal regularity of user visits and combines temporal signals with spatial and categorical features for next POI prediction.

sections.heading: MTNet.
sections.text: MTNet Hu et al. (2018) is a multi-task learning framework that jointly models next POI prediction, category prediction, and arrival time estimation. By sharing representations across related tasks, it captures richer user mobility patterns than single-task approaches.

sections.heading: STHGCN.
sections.text: STHGCN Yan et al. (2023) models higher-order spatial-temporal correlations among users and POIs through hypergraph convolutions. It constructs hyperedges that connect multiple POIs visited within the same trajectory, capturing group-level mobility patterns beyond pairwise transitions.

sections.heading: ROTAN.
sections.text: ROTAN Feng et al. (2024b) employs a rotation-based attention mechanism to model spatial relationships in next POI recommendation. It encodes geographic coordinates as rotation angles in the attention computation, enabling the model to directly reason about spatial proximity and directional patterns in user trajectories.

sections.heading: SpaceTime-GR.
sections.text: SpaceTime-GR Lin et al. (2025) is a space-time aware generative recommendation model that incorporates spatial and temporal encodings into the generative framework. It discretizes geographic coordinates and timestamps into token sequences, allowing the language model to jointly generate spatial-temporal-aware POI predictions.

sections.heading: LLM4POI.
sections.text: LLM4POI Li et al. (2024) reformulates next POI recommendation as a text generation task by serializing check-in trajectories into natural language prompts. It leverages the pre-trained knowledge of LLMs to understand location semantics through rich textual descriptions of POI names and categories.

sections.heading: GNPR-SID.
sections.text: GNPR-SID Wang et al. (2025) introduces discrete semantic identifiers to represent POIs, replacing verbose POI names with compact token sequences derived from clustering POI embeddings. This reduces input length and enables compositional generalization across POIs with shared semantic properties.

sections.heading: GA-LLM.
sections.text: GA-LLM Liu et al. (2025) injects geographic coordinates and POI-to-POI transition structures into the LLM-based recommendation framework. It encodes latitude-longitude information and spatial distance features directly into the prompt, enhancing the model’s awareness of geographic constraints in user mobility.

sections.heading: CoAST.
sections.text: CoAST Zhai et al. (2025) introduces semantic discrete identifiers combined with a cognitive alignment training strategy. It designs a multi-stage training pipeline that progressively aligns the LLM’s representations with spatial-temporal patterns in user trajectories.

sections.heading: ROS.
sections.text: ROS Lv et al. (2026) represents the current state-of-the-art in generative POI recommendation. It introduces Hierarchical Spatial Semantic IDs that encode both geographic locality (via S2 cell prefixes) and semantic similarity into compositional token sequences. ROS further proposes a Mobility Chain-of-Thought reasoning paradigm and spatial-guided reinforcement learning to enhance prediction accuracy. AWARE builds upon the same SID-equipped backbone as ROS, enabling a controlled comparison that isolates the contribution of world knowledge injection.

sections.heading: Appendix E Implementation Details
sections.text: Implementation Details. AWARE adopts Qwen3-4B Yang et al. (2025) as the generative backbone, with Spatial Semantic IDs derived from Qwen3-0.6B embeddings. To preserve the pretrained spatial reasoning capability while adapting to the knowledge-enriched input, we apply LoRA Hu et al. (2022) for parameter-efficient fine-tuning with rank r = 64 r=64 and scaling factor α = 128 \alpha=128 . The world knowledge is generated by prompting an LLM agent ( Qwen3-max ) with each user’s trajectory and temporal context prior to training. The agent retrieves external evidence via SerpAPI-backed web search with date-range filtering and page-level content extraction, capped at two parallel retrieval rounds per user. Output length is regulated by a rewrite-then-truncate cascade. For time-aware history selection, we set the periodic ratio β = 0.4 \beta=0.4 and the history budget L = 150 L=150 entries. Training is conducted for 2 epochs with a learning rate of 1e-4 on 8 × AMD-Instinct-MI308X-OAM 8\times\text{AMD-Instinct-MI308X-OAM} GPUs. For a fair comparison, we inherit all other hyperparameters from ROS Lv et al. (2026) . Temporal Fidelity. The evaluation benchmarks (Foursquare NYC/TKY, Gowalla-CA) span 2009–2013 and predate the training corpora of contemporary LLMs, risking contamination of historical-user narratives with present-day information. To prevent this, temporal grounding is enforced at three levels. (i) Prompt level: Π \Pi instructs the agent to treat the latest timestamp in 𝒮 u \mathcal{S}_{u} as “now” and to prefer archival sources over undated present-day pages. (ii) Tool level: every search query is rewritten to inject the target year and month as a date-range constraint, and results are pre-filtered by publication date. (iii) Synthesis level: a post-hoc verifier discards any claim not corroborated by a source dated within [ t − Δ , t + Δ ] [t-\Delta,\,t+\Delta] ( Δ = 30 \Delta=30 days). Under this regime, the injected world knowledge faithfully reflects the user’s original temporal and spatial context. A manual audit of 200 randomly sampled narratives confirms that event references are anchored within the target window.

sections.heading: Appendix F Case Study
sections.text: Figure 7: Case study on NYC. The user frequents a neighborhood area (37 visits) and a Caribbean restaurant (18 visits). ROS predicts Train Station from the recent trajectory, while AWARE correctly predicts Caribbean Restaurant . To illustrate how world knowledge captures intent beyond sequential patterns, we present a representative case in Figure 7 . On Saturday morning, ROS predicts Train Station based on the recent trajectory ending near a transit hub. AWARE instead correctly predicts Caribbean Restaurant , guided by the following world knowledge: “Contemporary data indicates that Caribbean eateries like Golden Krust were neighborhood staples …With cold weather prevailing, the user is likely seeking convenient, familiar services nearby, particularly warm Caribbean meals .” Behavioral priors further corroborate the prediction: POI frequency statistics rank Caribbean Restaurant as the user’s second most visited location, and transition patterns reveal 13 bidirectional trips between it and the nearby neighborhood area. This case illustrates how world knowledge provides the cultural why behind a visit, while behavioral priors supply the personalized where , together resolving predictions that sequential models cannot.

Email: lvdongyi@stu.xjtu.edu.cn Abstract Generative point-of-interest (POI) recommendation models based on large language models (LLMs) have shown promising results by formulating next POI prediction as a sequence generation task. However, the knowledge encoded in these models remains fixed after training, making them unable to perceive evolving real-world conditions that shape user mobility decisions, such as local events and cultural trends. To bridge this gap, we propose AWARE (Agent-based World knowledge Augmented REcommendation), which employs an LLM agent to generate location- and time-aware contextual narratives that capture regional cultural characteristics, seasonal trends, and ongoing events relevant to each user. Rather than introducing generic or noisy information, AWARE further anchors these narratives in each user’s behavioral context, grounding external world knowledge in personalized spatial-temporal patterns. Extensive experiments on three real-world datasets demonstrate that AWARE consistently outperforms competitive baselines, achieving up to 12.4% relative improvement. 1 Introduction With the proliferation of location-based social networks (LBSNs) and mobile devices, massive volumes of user check-in data have become available, enabling the study of human mobility at an unprecedented scale Gonzalez et al. (2008) . A central task in this domain is next point-of-interest (POI) recommendation : given a user’s historical check-in trajectory, predicting the most likely next location they will visit Li et al. (2024) ; Feng et al. (2024a) ; Halder et al. (2022) ; Zhong et al. (2025) . Accurate next POI prediction directly benefits real-world applications, including personalized navigation, location-aware advertising, and urban planning Zheng (2015) , and has attracted increasing attention from both academia and industry in recent years. Existing approaches have evolved from collaborative filtering and Markov chain models Feng et al. (2015) to recurrent and attention-based architectures Hochreiter and Schmidhuber (1997) ; Luo et al. (2021) ; Yang et al. (2022) ; Yan et al. (2023) that capture increasingly complex spatial-temporal dependencies. More recently, large language models (LLMs) Ding et al. (2026) ; Rajput et al. (2023) ; Chen et al. (2025) ; Jiang et al. (2026) ; Zhou et al. (2025) have given rise to generative POI recommendation Li et al. (2024) ; Wang et al. (2025) ; Liu et al. (2025) ; Lv et al. (2026) , which serializes check-in history into a natural language prompt and fine-tunes an LLM to directly generate the next POI. By exploiting rich textual representations rather than opaque ID embeddings, generative approaches achieve strong performance on next POI prediction benchmarks. Despite their promise, existing generative POI recommendation models share a critical limitation: once fine-tuned on historical data, they operate as static systems whose knowledge is entirely frozen at training time. This renders them unable to capture evolving real-world context, such as local events, cultural trends, and seasonal shifts, that fundamentally shapes user mobility decisions. For example, a user who routinely visits a gym on weekday evenings may instead attend a community fitness event at a nearby park; a static model, unaware of this event, would confidently predict the gym and fail. Without access to such external context, existing methods capture where users have been but not why they go next. To address this gap, we propose AWARE ( A gent-based W orld- A ugmented RE commendation), a framework that injects dynamic, personalized world knowledge into the generative recommendation pipeline (Figure 1 ). For each user’s activity region and time period, AWARE employs an LLM agent to synthesize contextual narratives, termed hotspot text , describing regional cultural characteristics, seasonal trends, and ongoing events. Unlike RAG, which returns pre-indexed documents irrespective of user identity, our agent reasons over each user’s mobility history to produce personalized narratives that distill relevant world context into actionable conclusions. To ensure the injected knowledge remains user-specific rather than generic, AWARE further anchors the hotspot text in behavioral signals such as frequently visited locations and habitual spatial transitions. 2 Background 2.1 Problem Formulation Let 𝒰 \mathcal{U} denote the set of users and 𝒫 \mathcal{P} the set of POIs. Each POI p ∈ 𝒫 p\in\mathcal{P} is associated with a name, a category, and geographic coordinates. A check-in ( u , p , t ) (u,p,t) records that user u u visited POI p p at time t t . For each user u u , the check-in history is an ordered sequence 𝒮 u = [ ( p 1 , t 1 ) , ( p 2 , t 2 ) , … , ( p n , t n ) ] \mathcal{S}_{u}=[(p_{1},t_{1}),(p_{2},t_{2}),\ldots,(p_{n},t_{n})] . The task is to predict the next POI p n + 1 p_{n+1} given 𝒮 u \mathcal{S}_{u} and the current time context. Figure 2: Overview of the AWARE framework. (1) An LLM agent retrieves external signals (e.g., news, events, festivals) and integrates them with user behavioral patterns to produce personalized narratives. (2) The pretrained GR model is fine-tuned with the acquired world knowledge to generate context-aware recommendations. 2.2 Generative POI Recommendation Recent work reframes next POI prediction as a text generation task Li et al. (2024) ; Wang et al. (2025) ; Liu et al. (2025) ; Lv et al. (2026) . A user’s check-in history is serialized into a structured prompt containing POI names, categories, timestamps, and geographic information. An LLM is then fine-tuned to generate the next POI as its output sequence. Formally, a prompt construction function ϕ ⁡ ( ⋅ ) \phi(\cdot) converts 𝒮 u \mathcal{S}_{u} into a textual input x = ϕ ⁡ ( 𝒮 u ) x=\phi(\mathcal{S}_{u}) , and the model is trained to maximize P ⁡ ( y ∣ x ) P(y\mid x) , where y y is the ground-truth next POI. This formulation enables the model to leverage pre-trained semantic knowledge about location names and categories, providing richer representations than ID-based. 2.3 Semantic ID Rather than representing POIs by raw names, which consume lengthy token sequences and lack structural relationships, recent work assigns each POI a compact Semantic ID (SID) Wang et al. (2025) . SID encodes each POI as a short compositional token sequence whose components capture different facets and can be shared across POIs: Coffee Shop, 1128 3rd Ave ⇒ \Rightarrow <a_29><b_31><c_20> Coffee Shop, 5 W 21st St ⇒ \Rightarrow <a_26><b_3><c_20> Both POIs share <c_20> due to their common category, while the remaining tokens capture individual identity. AWARE is agnostic to the POI representation scheme; in this work we adopt a SID-equipped generative backbone (details in Section 3 ). 2.4 World Knowledge for POI Recommendation In this work, world knowledge refers to dynamic, location-specific contextual information beyond check-in records, including regional cultural characteristics, local events, and seasonal trends. Such knowledge evolves continuously and often drives user mobility decisions, yet cannot be encoded statically within model parameters. We define world knowledge as w = 𝒜 ⁡ ( 𝒮 u , l , t ) w=\mathcal{A}(\mathcal{S}_{u},l,t) , where 𝒜 \mathcal{A} denotes an LLM agent, l l is the user’s activity region, and t t is a temporal context. Unlike generic knowledge retrieval, 𝒜 \mathcal{A} first analyzes the user’s mobility patterns from 𝒮 u \mathcal{S}_{u} , then incorporates real-world events and trends relevant to region l l at time t t . For example, given a user who commutes between Queens and Midtown Manhattan and has visited Yankee Stadium on weekends during April–May 2012, the agent may generate: “The user exhibits a commuting pattern between Queens and Midtown Manhattan. Combined with the Yankees’ home season in April–May, the user is likely interested in upcoming home games or nearby venues.” We term this output hotspot text , a personalized narrative that bridges user behavior with external world dynamics to reason about why a user is likely to visit certain POIs. 3 Methodology In this section, we present the AWARE framework (see Figure 2 ). We first describe the personalized world knowledge acquisition (Section 3.1 ), then introduce user-aware knowledge alignment (Section 3.2 ), and finally detail the context-aware generative inference (Section 3.3 ). 3.1 World Knowledge Acquisition Agent Existing generative POI models treat knowledge as static, yet user mobility is shaped by evolving real-world dynamics that no fixed-parameter model can capture. External sources such as news feeds, event calendars, and travel portals offer a natural remedy, but their content is vast and largely irrelevant to any individual user. This motivates AWARE’s design principle: leveraging each user’s behavioral patterns as an anchor for world knowledge selection, so that the distilled signals capture not only where users have been but why they are likely to go next. 3.1.1 Three-Stage Reasoning Strategy To this end, AWARE instantiates a tool-augmented LLM agent 𝒜 \mathcal{A} that, given a user’s trajectory 𝒮 u \mathcal{S}_{u} and the temporal–spatial context ( t , l ) (t,l) implied by the tail of the trajectory, is equipped with a retrieval toolbox ℛ = { web_search , web_fetch } \mathcal{R}=\{\texttt{web\_search},\,\texttt{web\_fetch}\} and produces a compact hotspot text: w = 𝒜 ⁡ ( 𝒮 u , t , l , ℛ , Π ) , w=\mathcal{A}\bigl(\mathcal{S}_{u},\,t,\,l\,;\,\mathcal{R},\,\Pi\bigr), (1) where Π \Pi denotes the system prompt that governs the agent’s reasoning protocol. The protocol decomposes into three sequential stages, with a detailed description provided below. Stage (i): Behavioral Profile Inference. The agent first parses 𝒮 u \mathcal{S}_{u} in chronological order and weights the tail of the sequence more heavily to identify the user’s active neighborhood l l , recurring interests (e.g., dining style, commute routine, fitness habits, nightlife preferences), and plausible near-term intent. This profile is retained as an internal anchor and never exposed verbatim in the final output, ensuring that downstream retrieval is driven by user-specific priors rather than generic demographic assumptions. Stage (ii): Constrained External Retrieval. Conditioned on the inferred profile, the agent formulates targeted web queries that jointly bind three constraints: geographic (restricted to l l and its surrounding neighborhoods), temporal (anchored at t t , with the target year and month embedded explicitly in every query), and thematic (the inferred interest categories). Retrieval proceeds iteratively: broader web_search calls first surface candidate event calendars, neighborhood guides, and news items, after which web_fetch verifies specific claims on the most informative pages. The agent is explicitly instructed to corroborate each substantive claim across at least two independent sources and to discard any signal that cannot be anchored to the target time window, which mitigates hallucinations inherited from the LLM’s parametric memory. Stage (iii): Grounded Synthesis. In the final stage, the agent weaves the internal behavioral anchor together with the verified external signals into a single coherent paragraph w w . The paragraph is required to interleave three elements in a tightly integrated manner: (a) what the user’s history suggests, (b) what regional context is salient at time t t , and (c) what POI categories or venue styles the user is most likely to seek next. Outputs that merely recite the trajectory, or that read as generic city guides disconnected from user behavior, are rejected by the format constraints in Π \Pi , ensuring that w w reads as a user-grounded contextual interpretation rather than a document summary. 3.1.2 Agent Instantiation and Prompt Design We instantiate 𝒜 \mathcal{A} with a large-capacity LLM ( Qwen3-max ) augmented with a web-retrieval toolbox ℛ \mathcal{R} that provides date-filtered web search and page-level content extraction. The system prompt Π \Pi encodes the three-stage protocol as explicit instructions and imposes three key constraints: (i) all factual claims must be grounded in retrieved evidence rather than parametric memory, (ii) the output must be a single coherent paragraph, and (iii) the length must not exceed a word budget M M , which can be adjusted according to application requirements. Beyond the reasoning protocol, Π \Pi encodes runtime guarantees for temporal fidelity, search-budget control, and output-length control. 3.1.3 Generation Quality Control Beyond the reasoning protocol, AWARE enforces three operational constraints on agent outputs, namely output-format control , tool-usage efficiency , and temporal fidelity , each implemented across prompt, tool, and post-hoc validation layers to forestall any single failure mode. Output-Format Control. Since the downstream GR model is prompt-length sensitive, we enforce the word budget M M via a prompt, validator, and truncator cascade: Π \Pi instructs the agent to cap w w at M M words and self-check length; if the validator detects | w | > M |w|>M , the agent is re-invoked with a brief rewrite instruction; any residual overshoot is hard-truncated. We instantiate two budgets, M = 80 M=80 and M = 150 M=150 , which anchor the informativeness versus noise trade-off in Section 4.5 . Tool Usage Efficiency. Since agent rollouts dominate preprocessing cost, Π \Pi caps retrieval at two rounds, a broad main round and an optional supplemental round for residual gaps, and encourages parallel rather than sequential queries within each round; our orchestrator dispatches them concurrently. A code-level guard hard-stops any attempt at a third round and forces synthesis, bounding per-user latency and cost. Temporal Fidelity. As the evaluation benchmarks span 2009 to 2013 and predate contemporary LLM training corpora, AWARE grounds the agent in the user’s own timeline: the latest timestamp in 𝒮 u \mathcal{S}_{u} is treated as “now,” every query is anchored to the target year and month, and documents lacking period-appropriate corroboration are discarded, ensuring that the injected knowledge reflects the user’s original temporal and spatial context. 3.2 User-Aware Knowledge Alignment Indiscriminate injection of world knowledge risks introducing noise. To ensure that external context is actionable for each user, AWARE aligns world knowledge with user-specific behavioral evidence through three complementary priors. Frequency-Based Behavioral Prior. We compute a frequency-ranked list of each user’s visited POIs: ℱ u = [ ( p 1 , c 1 , f 1 ) , ( p 2 , c 2 , f 2 ) , … ] \mathcal{F}_{u}=[(p_{1},c_{1},f_{1}),(p_{2},c_{2},f_{2}),\ldots] (2) where p i p_{i} denotes a POI, c i c_{i} its category, and f i f_{i} the visit count. This prior encodes long-term behavioral regularities and serves as a relevance filter: signals aligning with established patterns receive implicit reinforcement, while those lacking behavioral corroboration are down-weighted. Transition-Based Spatial Grounding. We model user mobility dynamics by extracting POI-to-POI transition statistics. For each POI p i p_{i} visited by user u u , we record the set of subsequent destinations and their frequencies: 𝒯 u ​ ( p i ) = { ( p j , n i ​ j ) } j = 1 | 𝒩 ⁡ ( p i ) | \mathcal{T}_{u}(p_{i})=\{(p_{j},n_{ij})\}_{j=1}^{|\mathcal{N}(p_{i})|} (3) where p j p_{j} is a destination POI and n i ​ j n_{ij} the transition count. Given the most recently visited POI, we select the top- k k most frequent transitions as spatial grounding signals, channeling world knowledge through the user’s movement structure. Periodic Temporal Modeling. User mobility often exhibits strong periodicity : behavior on Monday mornings is more predictive of next Monday than activity from the preceding weekend. To capture such long-range periodic evidence, AWARE reserves a fraction β \beta of the history budget for entries sharing the same day-of-week as the prediction target, filling the remaining slots with the most recent entries. This ensures that temporal knowledge from the agent (e.g., “Friday evening trends”) is paired with the user’s corresponding historical behavior. 3.3 Context-Aware Generative Inference Before describing how AWARE constructs its input, we briefly outline the generative recommendation (GR) pipeline. Each POI is assigned an SID by embedding its textual description through a pretrained language model and discretizing via hierarchical clustering. A geospatial prefix derived from S2 cells Google Inc. (2023) is prepended to encode geographic locality at multiple resolutions, enabling spatially proximate POIs to share prefix tokens. The model is trained to generate the ground-truth next POI’s SID given the user’s historical sequence, and autoregressively produces the predicted SID at inference time Lv et al. (2026) . Building on this pipeline, AWARE organizes the acquired knowledge (Sec. 3.2 ) into a structured prompt providing three complementary dimensions beyond the check-in sequence: x = ϕ ⁡ ( ℋ u , ℱ u , w , 𝒞 u , 𝒯 u ) x=\phi(\mathcal{H}_{u},\mathcal{F}_{u},w,\mathcal{C}_{u},\mathcal{T}_{u}) (4) where ℋ u \mathcal{H}_{u} denotes the time-aware historical trajectories, ℱ u \mathcal{F}_{u} the POI visit frequency statistics, w w the generated world knowledge, 𝒞 u \mathcal{C}_{u} the current trajectory to be continued, and 𝒯 u \mathcal{T}_{u} the transition pattern conditioned on the last visited POI. Prior POI recommendation work has leveraged geographic knowledge such as street-level addresses Lv et al. (2026) , category taxonomies Wang et al. (2025) , and spatial distance constraints Liu et al. (2025) . However, these sources are predominantly static and do not capture the dynamic real-world context that often drives user mobility decisions. LLM Agents for Information Acquisition. Agent-based approaches such as RecMind Wang et al. (2024) employ the LLM as the recommender itself, performing multi-step reasoning at inference time Yao et al. (2023) . While effective, this design couples reasoning cost with serving latency and forgoes the ability to learn fine-grained behavioral patterns from large-scale training data. Different from methods above, AWARE uses the LLM agent solely for offline knowledge acquisition, allowing the generative backbone to internalize dynamic world knowledge through supervised learning and adapt it to individual user contexts. 6 Conclusion We present AWARE, a framework that acquires world knowledge via an LLM agent, personalizes it through behavioral priors, and injects it into generative POI recommendation to capture context-dependent mobility intent. Experiments across multiple datasets show consistent gains over competitive baselines, and ablations confirm that the two signals are complementary, revealing not only where users have been but why they will go next. Limitations AWARE currently acquires world knowledge in an offline, pre-training stage: hotspot text is generated once per user and remains fixed throughout training and inference. While this design ensures zero additional latency at serving time, it cannot capture events that emerge after the knowledge acquisition pass. Extending the framework to support incremental or online knowledge refresh, where the agent periodically updates narratives in response to newly occurring events, would further improve temporal coverage. Additionally, the current agent relies on web search as its primary evidence source, which may offer uneven coverage across geographic regions and languages.
